ben-angel.bio: Ben Angel writes for entrepreneurs about the point where advice about productivity stops being useful. In *Unstoppable*, he starts with his own experience of fatigue and asks what happens when trying harder fails to solve the problem. The book follows his 90-day experiment with changes to his routine. His later book, *The Wolf Is at the Door*, turns to a different challenge for business owners: deciding which parts of their work to entrust to AI.

alisa-vitti.bio: Alisa Vitti founded FLO Living and wrote *WomanCode* and *In the FLO*. The second book takes the menstrual cycle as its organizing principle. Vitti walks readers through its phases and describes how she adjusts meals, exercise and work around them. Her term for that approach is “cycle syncing.”

aubrey-marcus.bio: Aubrey Marcus founded the fitness company Onnit and hosts long-form conversations on the *Aubrey Marcus Podcast*. His book *Own the Day, Own Your Life* is structured around a single day, following a reader from waking through meals, work, training and bedtime. It gives his ideas about performance a concrete setting: the ordinary decisions that recur tomorrow.

brad-stulberg.bio: Brad Stulberg writes about sustaining demanding work over time. He and running coach Steve Magness co-wrote *Peak Performance*, drawing parallels between athletic training and creative work, particularly the role of recovery between hard efforts. In *Master of Change*, Stulberg takes up a related question: how to keep a sense of direction when familiar routines fall apart.

chris-van-tulleken.bio: Chris van Tulleken is a British infectious-disease physician and broadcaster. In *Ultra-Processed People*, he uses his own experience eating a diet high in ultra-processed food as a starting point for reporting. The book follows the subject beyond ingredients to the companies that design, price and market the food people encounter every day.

conrad-smith.bio: Conrad Smith is the author credited on *Limitless Biohacking: Gain an Unfair Advantage*. The book presents biohacking for a general audience, framing personal experimentation around the pursuit of better performance. It is the work associated with Smith in this directory.

daniel-z-lieberman.bio: Daniel Z. Lieberman is a psychiatrist who co-wrote *The Molecule of More* with Michael E. Long. The book uses the difference between wanting something and enjoying it once it arrives to introduce dopamine. Its examples range from the anticipation of a new relationship to the persistence of an inventor chasing an idea.

david-mcraney.bio: David McRaney began *You Are Not So Smart* as a project about everyday errors in reasoning and developed it into a book and podcast. In *How Minds Change*, he interviews researchers and people who have reconsidered deeply held convictions. His reporting turns an abstract question about belief into a practical one about what happens during an actual conversation.

ed-yong.bio: Ed Yong is a science journalist whose books shift the reader’s sense of scale. *I Contain Multitudes* explores animals through the microbes that live alongside them. *An Immense World* takes the perspective of the animals themselves, asking how environments familiar to humans register to creatures that sense electric fields, vibrations or ultraviolet light.

elizabeth-blackburn.bio: Elizabeth Blackburn is a molecular biologist who studied telomeres, the protective structures at chromosome ends. She shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Carol Greider and Jack Szostak for discoveries about how chromosomes are protected by telomeres and the enzyme telomerase. She later co-wrote *The Telomere Effect* with psychologist Elissa Epel for a general audience.

eric-goodman.bio: Eric Goodman developed Foundation Training, a movement practice that teaches people to pay attention to how they bend, stand and carry weight. In *True to Form*, he brings those exercises out of a workout setting and into everyday tasks. A recurring example is the hip hinge, a movement most people repeat many times without thinking about it.

gerald-h-pollack.bio: Gerald H. Pollack is a bioengineering researcher at the University of Washington. His laboratory studies water near surfaces, including regions from which particles are excluded. In *The Fourth Phase of Water*, Pollack presents his interpretation of these observations and describes the experiments behind his proposed model.

gretchen-reynolds.bio: Gretchen Reynolds is a journalist who reports on exercise science. In *The First 20 Minutes*, she asks what exercise research can tell someone who simply wants to know how much to move and where to begin. She follows questions about endurance, strength and recovery from laboratory experiments into the choices people make on an ordinary walk or run.

james-lee.bio: James Lee wrote *The Biohacking Manifesto*, a guide to personal experimentation with health and longevity. It brings anti-aging research and neuroscience together under a practical question: which everyday routines might a reader choose to investigate? The directory entry refers specifically to the writer credited on this book.

jevan-pradas.bio: Jevan Pradas wrote *The Awakened Ape*, which puts contemplative practice in conversation with evolutionary psychology. He asks how a mind shaped under earlier living conditions responds to modern sources of stimulation, then explores meditation and attention through that lens. The book moves between an argument about human behavior and exercises readers can try.

john-j-ratey.bio: John J. Ratey is a psychiatrist and the author, with Eric Hagerman, of *Spark*. The book examines exercise through its effects on learning, attention and mood. One of its central stories comes from a school physical-education program, where the question was what happened in the classroom after students had been active.

joe-dispenza.bio: Joe Dispenza writes and leads workshops on meditation, attention and personal change. In *Becoming Supernatural*, he combines accounts from workshop participants with guided practices involving visualization and focused attention. The book presents his own interpretation of those experiences and the ideas that shape his workshops.

kristen-willeumier.bio: Kristen Willeumier is a neuroscientist and the author of *Biohack Your Brain*. She translates her interest in brain imaging and cognition into questions about sleep, movement, food and attention. The book is written for readers interested in how their daily routines relate to the brain across a lifetime.

lee-know.bio: Lee Know writes about mitochondria, the structures inside cells that convert energy from nutrients into forms the body can use. His book *Mitochondria and the Future of Medicine* starts with that cellular machinery and follows its possible implications for aging and chronic illness. Its subject is the connection between small-scale biochemistry and whole-body physiology.

martin-bjergegaard.bio: Martin Bjergegaard is a Danish entrepreneur who co-wrote *Winning Without Losing* with Jordan Milne. They interviewed founders about how they protect time for relationships, rest and interests outside their businesses. The book organizes those conversations into short accounts of decisions about the working day.

maximilian-gotzler.bio: Maximilian Gotzler is a German writer, former competitive basketball player and founder of Flowgrade. His book *Biohacking – Optimiere dich selbst* draws on his interest in athletic performance to explore sleep, energy and daily routines. Through Flowgrade he also interviews practitioners about how they measure and interpret their own experiments.

michael-breus.bio: Michael Breus is a clinical psychologist specializing in sleep. In *The Power of When*, he asks how a person’s preferred timing for waking, working and sleeping might inform the shape of their day. He uses four animal-named chronotypes as a way for readers to follow the book’s scheduling advice.

molly-maloof.bio: Molly Maloof is a physician and the author of *The Spark Factor*. She approaches health through the question of energy: how cells produce it and how fatigue feels in daily life. The book connects her interest in mitochondria with chapters on food, exercise, stress and social connection, written with women readers in mind.

olli-sovijrvi.bio: Olli Sovijärvi is a Finnish physician and co-author of the *Biohacker’s Handbook*, alongside Teemu Arina and Jaakko Halmetoja. The handbook organizes material around sleep, nutrition, exercise, work and the mind. Sovijärvi brings a medical perspective to the team’s accounts of measurement and personal experimentation.

patrick-mckeown.bio: Patrick McKeown is a breathing educator who developed the Oxygen Advantage program. In *The Oxygen Advantage*, he discusses how breathing patterns change between rest and exercise, with particular attention to nasal breathing. His teaching pairs explanations of breathing mechanics with drills that readers and athletes can practice.

rhonda-patrick.bio: Rhonda Patrick is a biomedical scientist and co-founder of FoundMyFitness. She uses long-form interviews and research explainers to examine questions about micronutrients, exercise, heat exposure and aging. A recurring feature of her work is following a proposed mechanism from what happens inside a cell to what researchers can actually measure in people.

richard-roper.bio: Richard Roper is a British novelist and editor. His debut, *How Not to Die Alone*, follows a council employee whose job brings him into the homes of people who have died alone. A misunderstanding about his own family life grows into a story about isolation, friendship and the difficulty of admitting that one needs other people.

robb-wolf.bio: Robb Wolf is the author of *The Paleo Solution* and *Wired to Eat*. After writing about ancestral diets, he turned his attention to differences in how individuals respond to food. In *Wired to Eat*, he asks readers to track their own responses to particular meals as part of his approach to appetite and eating habits.

sandra-kahn.bio: Sandra Kahn is an orthodontist who co-wrote *Jaws: The Story of a Hidden Epidemic* with biologist Paul R. Ehrlich. They examine how jaws develop and ask what changes in diet, chewing and breathing might mean for facial growth. The book brings a practitioner’s questions about crowded teeth into a wider discussion of human development.

scott-carney.bio: Scott Carney is an investigative journalist whose reporting often puts him inside the practices he studies. For *What Doesn’t Kill Us*, he trained with Wim Hof and investigated claims about breathing exercises and cold exposure. The book combines the story of that experience with interviews and reporting on environmental stress.

shane-snow.bio: Shane Snow is a journalist and entrepreneur who wrote *Smartcuts*. He looks at cases in which people made unusually rapid progress and asks which decisions helped them do so. His later book *Dream Teams* shifts the focus from the individual to groups, exploring why some teams make productive use of disagreement.

shawn-stevenson.bio: Shawn Stevenson hosts *The Model Health Show* and wrote *Sleep Smarter*. His book treats bedtime as the end of a sequence that begins much earlier, with light exposure, movement and the timing of daily activities. Each chapter connects a question about sleep to a routine the reader can examine.

simone-janen.bio: Simone Janßen is the author of the German-language book *Die Reenergize-Formel*. Its subtitle, *Der evolutionäre Baukasten für Energie und Glück*, describes her organizing idea: a toolkit for thinking about energy and well-being through an evolutionary lens. The book is her contribution to the directory’s German-language reading list.

steven-kotler.bio: Steven Kotler writes about performance and the experience psychologists call flow. For *The Rise of Superman*, he reported on action and adventure athletes working at the limits of their sports. Their accounts give him a way to investigate concentration, the perception of risk and why time can feel different during an absorbing task.

thad-a-polk.bio: Thad A. Polk is a cognitive neuroscientist at the University of Michigan. His laboratory uses behavioral experiments and brain imaging to study cognition, including how abilities change with age. In his lecture series *The Addictive Brain*, he introduces a broader audience to the connections between learning, reward and compulsive behavior.

travis-christofferson.bio: Travis Christofferson is a science writer and the author of *Tripping Over the Truth*. He follows the history of a debate about cancer: what researchers can explain by looking at changes in cellular metabolism. The book is a narrative account of that research and of the scientists who pursued the metabolic hypothesis.

will-bulsiewicz.bio: Will Bulsiewicz is a gastroenterologist who writes for a general audience about the gut microbiome. In *Fiber Fueled*, he uses the diversity of plant foods as a starting point for explaining what intestinal microbes do with dietary fiber. His follow-up cookbook translates the same topic into recipes and meal planning.

olli-sovijrviteemu-arinajaakko-halmetoja.bio: The *Biohacker’s Handbook* is a collaboration between physician Olli Sovijärvi, technology writer Teemu Arina and nutrition specialist Jaakko Halmetoja. The three authors bring their different perspectives to the same five subjects: sleep, nutrition, exercise, work and the mind. This entry credits the team behind the handbook.

teemu-arinaolli-sovijrvijaakko-halmetoja.bio: Teemu Arina, Olli Sovijärvi and Jaakko Halmetoja are the Finnish writing team credited on *The Optimized Human*. Their collaboration also produced the *Biohacker’s Handbook*. Their work brings technology, medicine and nutrition together around questions about everyday routines and the tools people use to measure them.

teemu-arinaolli-sovijrvi.bio: Teemu Arina and Olli Sovijärvi are Finnish collaborators on books about self-tracking and everyday health. Arina approaches the subject through technology and Sovijärvi through medicine. This entry credits the pair for *Biohacker’s Flu Guide*, distinct from their three-author collaboration on the *Biohacker’s Handbook*.
